subject: typewriter
pitch: A 1930s typewriter in glossy racing green. Round keys with cream letters on chrome rims in four staggered rows, a semicircle of thin type bars behind them, a chrome carriage return lever, a black platen roller with a sheet of paper half typed, and a small brass maker's badge on the front.
reasoning:
I'm planning to write a TypeScript module using the builder SDK, sticking to known APIs like joint, part, rod, slab, extrude, lathe, and decal, with careful placement options such as position, bone, aim, and orientation.

Since dir-based orientation is ambiguous, I'll pre-rotate geometries myself before placing them, and keep a single root joint since parts default to the nearest bone. For the keycaps, I'm deciding to model them as chrome rim rings with a dark body and a small cream glyph shape to represent the letter, since there's no text/SVG helper to rely on.

Now I'm laying out the overall dimensions and body structure: a plinth base with chrome feet, a lower body box, and a sloped front keyboard deck, all sized and positioned to form the classic typewriter silhouette.

Working out the deck's tilt angle and vertical rise so keys sit correctly along the slope, computing the rotation math needed to orient the deck's surface normal toward the front-upper direction.

Now I'm laying out the key rows in a staggered grid, assigning z-positions, spacing, and per-row key counts to fit the deck's width.

Each key gets a rim and cap cylinder positioned along the tilted surface normal, with a thin stem below. I'm also building the deck as a tilted box and figuring out where to anchor the lower body to cover underneath it.

Working out the rear block dimensions so it meets the deck surface cleanly, then sketching the type basket as a semicircular arc of thin rods radiating outward from a central pivot point above the rear block.

I'm unsure of the exact rod/spike API signature, so I'll fall back on computing orientation manually with a quaternion derived from the direction vector, applying it to the geometry rather than relying on undocumented helper methods.

I'll build a helper function that constructs a cylinder between two points by orienting via quaternion and translating to the midpoint, then pass it to the part system with explicit position and bone assignment. For the bars I'm also planning small box tips, a partial torus for the flat chrome rest ring, and a chrome cylinder as the type guide hub.

Now I'm working out the carriage layout: chrome rail boxes spanning the width, a black cylindrical platen, and the type bars arcing from a rear hub toward it. I'm not being too physically strict about exact collision-free placement, just roughing out plausible coordinates for the platen, hub, and bar radius so the assembly reads correctly.

I'm adding chrome end cap knobs at the platen ends, a carriage return lever arcing up from the left side with a black bakelite ball tip, and a tilted paper sheet emerging from behind the platen standing vertically.

I'm working out how the paper should curve as it wraps from behind the platen, up and over the top, then hangs down slightly in front, positioning the segments so the text-bearing face points toward the viewer.

I'm placing the typed lines in the lower portion near the platen, leaving the upper part of the sheet blank, and tilting the paper slightly backward to make the half-typed look believable.

I'm adding a brass maker's badge on the front panel below the keys, shaping it as a flattened oval disc with an inner darker ring, sized to fit within the panel area around y 0.085, z 0.19.

Now I'm laying out the four keyboard rows at z-depths of roughly 0.16, 0.123, 0.086, and 0.049, with a chrome spacebar positioned on the front lip near z=0.19, adjusting spacing so everything fits within the deck's front-to-back span.

Working out the key stagger offsets per row (alternating small shifts) and column counts (10,10,9,9), keeping each row's total width under the 0.34 deck limit. For the individual key construction, I'm defining a thin chrome stem cylinder embedded under each cap plus a surrounding rim cylinder sitting slightly above it.

Now I'm placing a dark cap cylinder inside the chrome rim so it protrudes just a bit above the rim edge, matching the "cream letters on chrome rims" spec. Then I'm planning the cream letter glyphs themselves -- building simple block-letter shapes (T, L, H, I, F, E) out of small bar segments positioned on top of each cap, picking orientation and layout per key.

Defining letter glyph templates...

Settling on the color palette: chrome, racing green, cream, black, and brass tones. I'm also planning decorative trim details like a chrome strip along the base and small ribbon spool discs near the rear, checking their positions don't collide with the semi-circular bars.

Working through the ribbon spool design with chrome flanges, a black ribbon core, and chrome hub, while deciding whether to add a pinstripe accent along the lower body sides in cream or brass.

I'm adding chrome corner strips along the front deck edges, then placing a two-segment chrome carriage return lever with a black ball end at its tip, and now I'm positioning the 27 type bars radiating from a central hub with azimuth angles spanning -78° to 78°.

Still writing bar geometry...

Working out the hoop radius at that height, then moving to the rear block: posts, carriage rail, and end plates sized and positioned, with the platen spanning between them.

Adding knobs, chrome rails, and considering the paper bail placement relative to the platen, deciding to skip the bail for now since it may overlap the paper feed path.

For the paper itself, I'm sketching it running vertically from about y=0.31 to 0.50, width 0.21, with a handful of text lines positioned a bit above center and blank space above that.

I'm deciding to skip the subtle tilt/curl rotation on the paper for simplicity, keeping the base model height capped around 0.5 so nothing extends above the paper top. Now I'm setting up the root joint of the structure at a low origin point and working out how the base part should attach to it.

I'm defining helper functions that build geometry centered at the origin, apply rotations when needed, then position the final part using the "at" offset -- box shapes get optional X-rotation before placement, and I'm starting similar logic for cylinders to construct rods between points. Writing helper functions...

Still positioning key geometry layers...

Checking whether the badge overlaps the deck lip, I realize the proportions are too tight, so I'm resizing the lower body to be taller with a small gap for chrome feet underneath, giving the badge more breathing room.

For the spacebar, I'm positioning it along the surface with its own rotation offset and chrome supports, and I decide to write my own random number generator rather than rely on an external one to avoid uncertainty about its interface.

Adding small chrome side plates to the rear block, skipping tabulator keys for now, and moving on to writing the actual code.
